utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, especially the Presiding Judge. Good morning to the Defence and the Prosecution. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Komad. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, before you commence your evidence, I must let you know a certain Rule that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Komad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Komad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Komad.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you to pause between our interventions, that is to say to speak slowly so as to have everything in the record. Can you tell us tell us whether you provided a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please have in e-court 1D7981.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid the e-court is still not working or properly functioning, so shall we put the statement on the ELMO? But if it is the case of statement, given that we all have the statement, it would be sufficient to provide the witness with his statement in hard copy. Mr. Komad, do you have your statement with you now? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was just noting if e-court is a problem, then we're just deferring the need to attend to it. We'll obviously need to have a functioning e-court before we get to cross-examination, perhaps even before the remainder of examination-in-chief. I just don't know the extent of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will inquire of the registrar whether it is a problem of Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I just heard from the registrar is that the old documents that is already in e-court have no problem, but the problem is with the new document that is to be uploaded on the e-court. So let's see how we can manage with this system. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This again raises the issue of my ability to upload documents, much like the Prosecution can. That will significantly reduce the problems, but nevertheless, we'll work this way. Can we then have the English version on the ELMO, and I will ask Mr. Komad, with the approval of the Chamber, to have a look at the hard copy of his statement that's before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, can you see the English version on the screen of the statement you provided?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read this statement and signed it?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement accurately reflect everything you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I'd like to correct something in the text, though, in item 2 where it is stated the teachers of Muslim ethnicity and professors working at civilian universities should be the professors working at civilian schools rather than religious schools. So secular schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's accepted. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Well, perhaps only a few technical matters. On the next page, item 5, it says number 4. That's where your apartment was, but it was at Sutjeska number 2. And in item 21, it says they wanted Banja Luka to be the centre of the Serb people instead of Pale. It should be Sarajevo, because that was -- instead of Banja Luka it should be Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Save for the corrections, is everything else recorded accurately?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly be asked to pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It shouldn't be -- instead of Pale it should be -- instead of Banja Luka, it should be -- instead of Sarajevo. Banja Luka to be instead of Sarajevo. Because Pale were a part of Sarajevo, Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that clear? The word "Pale" should be replaced with "Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: That's what I had in mind, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, having in mind the corrections you have just kindly mentioned, does the rest truthfully reflect your words?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you in the courtroom today would your answers be basically the same?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes. The gist of it would be the same.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, I seek to tender this statement as part of the 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. There's one small section that arguably fell within the Court's previous guidance, but it was very brief and so I don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit the statement as well as the four associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 92 ter statement 1D7981 will be Exhibit D3198, and the remaining four associated exhibits will be Exhibits D31992 to Exhibits 33201.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will read out a summary of Mr. Trifko Komad's statement in the English language. [In English] Mr. Trifko Komad worked from 1986 to the outbreak of war in the republican conference of the Socialist Alliance of B and H, in charge of issues related to religious communities. For some time he also worked on issues of the People's Defence. After the founding of the SDS, he became a member of the Main and Executive Boards. In late 1992, he became a member of the office of the Republika Srpska in Belgrade from where he retired. Trifko Komad saw that the Islamic and Catholic religious communities had enormous influence on social trends and politics in B and H. The influence on both religions could be seen throughout BH. However, the Orthodox religious group had a smaller standing. Even before the establishment of the SDS, Islamic fundamentalists were organising themselves and conducting monitoring exercises on cafes and many Serbs were scared about the developing situation before the establishment of the SDS. Due to his position, Trifko Komad was asked to comment upon the issue regarding Serbian ethnicity in a number of political circumstances. Trifko Komad was present at meetings in which the difficult position of the Serbs in BH, the protection of the Serbian people and plans for the future were discussed. At first point the first clashes between Croats and Serbs had already taken place and other parties had been established. Despite the previous establishment of the SDA and HDZ, there was a huge resistance in BH to the Serbian people organising themselves and therefore this could not be done publicly. In addition, Serbian people feared retribution in response to organising politically. When the Serbs were established -- the SDS was established in the -- it was for Yugoslavia and for the equal treatment of the Serbian people in the BH and Yugoslavia. Trifko Komad considers that the party was led by the Serbian people and their wishes which were considered by the leadership of the SDS. Following multi-party elections, when a coalition was formed it was clear that the other parties were breaching the coalition agreement regarding the appointments of the staff in the BH governmental bodies which led to a loss of confidence in the truthfulness of the SDA's claims. The SDS advocated constitutionality and legality in its activity. However, other parties acted in illegal and unconstitutional ways. Muslim party leaders, presidents of municipalities and municipal governments where Serbs were in power were invited to the SDS annual party conference in July 1991 as guests to encourage co-existence and joint action in BH. Many people were allowed to participate in meetings and media employees were also invited. Unfortunately, there was a lack of discipline in the local level of the party and the local leadership were rather autonomous in their work, leading to inter-party clashes. Trifko Komad was aware that the SDS wished to avoid bloodshed and war in BH at all costs. Due to the escalation of the situation in Sarajevo, he left in April 1992 with his son but only just managed to get his wife out soon after. Both his parents were persecuted in Sarajevo, which led them to deaths. His sister was also targeted in a hit and run incident. Trifko Komad -- Trifko Komad considers that due to his political affiliation. Crisis Staffs were established in municipalities where there was the greatest danger of the clashes breaking out. They were established to prevent clashes and protect the population, not to persecute the Muslims and Croat population. When hostilities broke out, the Crisis Staffs were left to their own devices, and in the majority of the Serbian authorities did not have any information about their work. Communication was interrupted and local organs were operating autonomously, so wartime commissions were introduced to link the republican government to the local branches including Pale. The SDS suspended its activity when fighting broke out to avoid the possibility of the party using its power to influence the work of the state organs. Following this, Mr. Trifko Komad escorted humanitarian aid convoys through Serbian territory. There were instances when convoys were stopped by armed Serbian forces and many members of the SDS fought for humanitarian aid to be delivered unhindered to the Muslims and Croats. The general position was that the Muslims and members of all other ethnic groups must be guaranteed all civil and other rights. Dr. Karadzic personally stopped the requesting -- and requested -- supported and requested that the Muslims do not move away from Janja and other places in Republika Srpska and became integrated -- instead to be integrated in population. And that is the summary and at that moment I do not have questions for Mr. Komad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Komad, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning to the Bench. Good morning to all. Good morning, Mr. Komad.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, at paragraph 9 of your statement, you state that after the inaugural conference of the SDS, which I believe was in July of 1990, you became a member of the Main Board and the Executive Board and the political council. In that respect, I'd like to look at a few documents or indicate to you that we have in evidence a few documents, including the following: D1275 reflect the minutes of the Executive Board of the SDS held on 6 September 1991. It lists at page 2 the members present, including Mr. Dukic, the President of the Executive Board, Mr. Neskovic and others, and then states in the subsequent paragraph that apart from the members of the Executive Board, the following attended, and that includes your name along with Jovan Turanjanin. Similarly at P25 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you mean to show the document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's in evidence, Mr. President, I'm not sure based on the question it will be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Similarly at P2584, a meeting of the Executive Board that took place ten days later on the 16th, it indicates before the agenda items are discussed the members of the Executive Board who were present and states further also in attendance were Trifko Komad and Jovan Turanjanin, secretaries of the party services of the SDS BH. Now, is it correct, therefore, Mr. Komad, that you were not a member of the Executive Board but you were secretary of party services serving the members of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No. I was the secretary of the Executive Board, and you can find that in certain documents. The secretary of the Executive Board is at the same time a member of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I take it then that you don't have an explanation for the distinction that is made in the minutes of the Executive Board between the members of the Executive Board and other persons such as yourself as they are listed who are also in attendance and indicated as I said earlier, secretary of the party services?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I can't comment on that, but I claim that I was the secretary of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Similarly with respect to the -- your Main Board membership, I wanted to look quickly at 65 ter 00698, which is a stenogram taken at the 12 July 1991 session of the SDS party, and although there is a good deal of discussion, I wanted to turn directly to pages 87 through 93 of the English, and pages 107 through 114 of the B/C/S that reflect the election of the SDS BM Main Board for -- and goes through it in various reasons. So if -- in various segments. So if we look first at page 87, we see the election of persons from the Herzegovina region including in Mr. Vucurevic, Mr. Kozic, and Mr. Nadezdin. Similarly for Stara Herzegovina. As we turn the page we see the election of people from Romanija including Mr. Kusic and Mr. Zugic. Semberija, Birac, Tuzla, Central Bosnia. And please pay attention to the names, many of whom the Court will be familiar with. On to Western Bosnia, south-western Bosnia, Bosnian Krajina. And then finally we see at pages 92 and 93 additional persons elected including Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Najdanovic, Mr. Buha, Mr. Toholj, Mr. Neskovic, and Mr. Saric. And then at the bottom of page 93, we see that Mr. Karadzic has been nominated as President of the SDS. He is the only candidate, and it appears to have been a unanimous vote. That -- by the way, that segment in B/C/S is at page 114, but I noted that the pages were inverted, so I think it goes in reverse order from 19 -- immediately jumps from 113 to 118 or 119 and then back counting down to 114 which is why you may not see it on that page. None of these names, Mr. Komad, are yours from any of those regions, so it appears that as indicated with the Executive Board that you are not listed as someone who was a member of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Can I explain? Under the statute, in addition to the nominees who are elected, the President of the party had a discretionary right to co-opt, I can't remember exactly how many but I think it's seven or eight people, and I was among those people co-opted into the Executive Board by the president of the party, and if you're talking about the Assembly on the 12th of July 1991, you can look it up in the statute. I -- it is I who provide the explanation of the statute as well as the programme, the platform of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Komad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender 65 ter 00698. I realise, Mr. President, there's a reference to those last pages, and the Court's previous guidance might have us just admitting those. I'm just at the Court's discretion. But given the nature of documents we've previously admitted, I'm more than happy to have the entirety of the document admitted and imagine that the Defence will probably feel the same way about this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would prefer the whole document be admitted. It's of the kind of document such as Assembly sessions that we've admitted in the past in their entirety, and so it could be useful to have it all admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. In the circumstances, we admit it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6243, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's one thing you'd like to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I just want to correct the record. The fourth associated exhibit will be Exhibit D3202. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just -- I don't think part of the answer of Mr. Komad was not recorded, that he was co-opted also into the Main Board, not only into the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Komad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing. The secretary for the Executive Board was an opening, and the description of the opening made it clear that it would also be a member of the Main Board and that's the opening I was running for, and I confirm what Mr. -- President Karadzic just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, at paragraph 17 and 18 of your statement, you refer to the plebiscite, and I just wanted to clarify one aspect of the plebiscite. So it is correct that the plebiscite ballots consisted of two different ballots with different colours, one for Serbs, one for non-Serbs, and with two different texts, one for Serbs and non-Serbs. And in that respect, if we could look quickly at 65 ter 17542. That's the meeting of the Executive Board of the 25th of October, 1991, and if we turn the page, we will see that it reveals that following the debate it was concluded that whilst observing organisational and technical requirements, two kinds of ballot papers should be printed out, blue ones for the citizens of the Serbian nationality and yellow ones for other nationalities. Can you confirm that that was the case, Mr. Komad, with respect to the plebiscite ballot?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And similarly if we call up quickly 65 ter 06621 and 06622 --

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Just one thing. Please, can I say something about the text? You also asked about the text, about the wording, was it the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you two documents with respect to the text right now, Mr. Komad. So you'll see on the screen 65 ter 06621 and then 06622. And while it's being called up, I'll describe briefly the difference. 06621 provides in Cyrillic: "Do you agree with the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian people," et cetera, "that the Serbian people remain in the common state of Yugoslavia with Serbia, Montenegro, SAO Krajina, SAO Slavonia Baranja," et cetera. And 06622 for non-Serbs in Latin Scripps states: "Do you vote for Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain as a republic with equal rights in the common state of Yugoslavia?"

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: This second text was also an official text for voters, members of all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender those documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those documents being?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not the previous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, and also 65 ter 17542, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit them all.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 17542 will be Exhibit P6244, 06621 will be Exhibit P6245, and 06622 will be Exhibit P6246.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 30, Mr. Komad, you dispute an adjudicated fact which stated that on 21 November 1991, the Bosnian Serb Assembly proclaimed as part of the territory of federal Yugoslavia all those municipalities, communes, and settlements where a majority of registered citizens of Serb nationality voted in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia, and you make the point about the basic socio-political community being the local community. With respect to your dispute of that adjudicated fact, can we turn to 1D20085. That will be a decision taken at the November 21st 1991 session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, which states in its first paragraph the territories of municipalities, local communities, and populated places in which -- in which more than 50 per cent of the Serbian electorate voted for the same joint state, and then we see in the last portion of that paragraph, "... shall be considered the territory of the federal state of Yugoslavia." Now, with insignificant differences, that decision reflects the text of the adjudicated fact that you disputed, does it not?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, may I explain my own position? According to earlier regulations and the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia, a local commune was defined as the basic socio-political entity. We had encountered cases where municipalities were split in that period, and I quoted the example of Neum which separated itself from Capljina, the example of Milici which split from Vlasenica. Janja was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- you're explaining is exactly what you state in your statement and which is already before the Court. My point was that you are -- you disputed this fact, and that fact is reflected in precisely in this decision. Now, you may have an explanation about what you consider to be the basic socio-political unit and how this might otherwise have been written, but you've accepted that this decision, in fact, was made, as we can see in the text, and that was the point I wanted to bring to the Court. So it's not necessary for you to repeat the text of the information -- the text of your statement and the information you provided there.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I tender 1D20085, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6247, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, at paragraph 23 of your statement, you briefly describe your information about the Variant A and B document, which as you indicate in paragraph 23 is extremely limited. Now, you also say at paragraph 11 that you were often present at the sessions of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. Do you recall whether you were present at the sixth session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly held on the 26th of January, 1992, that's P1349, at which following discussions about the need for action in the face of the apparent developments toward a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Cizmovic stated the following at page 13: "To solve this problem I propose that we begin with an urgent operationalisation and a declaration on the establishment and promulgation of the Serbian Republic of BiH. Tasks set out in the instructions of 19 December 1991 should be carried out." So there in front of everybody at the Assembly Mr. Cizmovic made an explicit reference to the 19 December document which reflected the Variants A and B and the first and second level. So notwithstanding the fact that everyone in the Assembly was reminded about it, is it still your position that you, Mr. Komad, knew nothing about it other than what you say in paragraph 23?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No, nothing else. I believe I probably did not attend that Assembly session. If I had been there, I would have probably remembered this. I said before it was not my obligation to be -- attend every session. I attended from time to time. The only thing I would like to say is that the document you talk about was not before the organs of the party, and it was not endorsed by the organs of the party. If it had been, it would have been in the protocol. It would have been entered in the log-book. It would have had a stamp. It would have been officialised. So I stand by the statement I have given.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, the president of the party would appear to be a fairly important organ of the party. Were you not present at the session of the deputies club on the 14th of February, 1992, when Mr. Karadzic spoke and made four separate references to the Variant A and B document, including asking the audience whether they remembered what he was discussing and getting the response we know, and concluding at page 22 of P00012, "That is why we called you today, to intensify, to introduce the second level and to intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and on every single millimetre of our territory." And for the benefit of the Court and the party, those individual references are found at pages 5, 7, 17, and 25 of the English and pages 4, 5, 12, and 18 of the B/C/S. Do you claim, Mr. Komad, that despite the fact again that everyone at that extended meeting of the -- everyone at that extended meeting of the deputies club was aware of the Variant A and B document but you were not aware of it?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, Mr. Komad, you -- that document which, among other things, called for the establishment of Crisis Staffs, and you did acknowledge that the party did create Crisis Staffs at paragraph 26. You also state at paragraph 27 that the party suspended its work following the outbreak of hostilities. In that connection, I wanted to ask you how quickly you claim that the party suspended its work after the outbreak of hostilities? And I take it, by the way, that you considered the outbreak of hostilities to be at the beginning of April. If you consider otherwise, let us know.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I believe too, with the proviso that the party was the initiator as far as the Crisis Staffs were concerned, but they were established by municipal authorities, by municipal governments, whereas the party was a political organisation and the initiator of that activity, but it was not the party that carried it out in all territories. That was done by municipal and local authorities. As for when the work of the party was put on hold, I believe it was May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Or June perhaps. May or June. I cannot remember the exact time. And that's what I said in the statement, that Mr. President called me and informed me of the decision to put the work of the party on hold.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. But not before the party attempted to ensure the transition from party Crisis Staffs into War Presidencies or War Commissions as had been ordered by the republic level RS authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, because the war was already going on. The state of war was imposed, so it's possible that the decision was not implemented in all the territories at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's reflected in P2608, a document that you sent on the 31st of May, 1992, as the secretary of the Executive Committee to various parts of RS authorities, specifically the SAOs, Herzegovina, Romanija, Birac, and Semberija, advising them that the decision of the republic authorities had been made, that War Commissions will be set up. Actually, in this document you refer both to War Commissions and War Presidencies indistinguishably. Tell them to continue performing their functions, and if they have any suggestions, remarks, or difficulties regarding implementation to contact the Presidency. That is Mr. Karadzic as president of the Presidency directly; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at -- in part of your statement you refer to events in Trebinje, that's paragraph 20 of your statement, and the involvement of the SDS republic level with events there. The Trial Chamber, Mr. Komad, has in fact received quite a bit of evidence about what happened in Trebinje during that period of time, and I'd like to confirm the details of what happened with you or challenge the full accuracy of your account with the evidence the Court has received. So first of all, Mr. -- let me march through that with you step-by-step, Mr. Komad. First of all, as we know from P6228, on the 2nd of September Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Vucurevic talked about a problem that Vucurevic was having with, among others, Grubac and Borkin [phoen]. And Dr. Karadzic told Mr. Vucurevic at page 3 of that document: "Who is not following our politics can go to another party." On the subsequent page Mr. Vucurevic begged him to come that same week, and at page 9 of that document Mr. Karadzic told him: "Don't you worry, we will finish it." You don't have any reason to dispute that that happened. That's an intercepted telephone conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Vucurevic which the Court has received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The next day, and that's found at P6229, Mr. Vucurevic continued to express concerns. Mr. Karadzic again told him not to worry, he would resolve it, saying: "We won't have anyone eating shit under our banner." That's at page 7. And assured Mr. Vucurevic that: "Momo and I will come. We will bring it all to an end." That's at page 8. And again you have no reason to dispute that chronology I take it, Mr. Komad.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I don't know what they said to each other. I cannot confirm whether it's correct or not, but I suppose if it's an intercept, then -- I can see here on the display that that's the subject of their discussion, but I cannot confirm either yes or no. I suppose it's true, because I cannot know what they talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Komad, you're -- you were involved in this according to your own statement, and you paint these events as somehow being a --

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- failed effort by Mr. Karadzic but a triumph on your part because somehow, as you painted, you had to intervene and therefore succeeded where Mr. Karadzic could not. So I want to continue with this chronology. On the 6th of September, according -- as we see from P2544, Mr. Karadzic spoke to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And although the English translation of this document has the date sometime in December, we received evidence long ago that clarified that date as being the 6th of September, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic told Milosevic: "I've just been to Trebinje and sacked some fools. They wanted to replace my man Bozo Vucurevic. When I made that null and void last night, I kicked them out, brought other people into the party and so on." And he explains the municipal government collapsed. That's at page 3 through 4 of 2544. Now, similarly, we have the minutes of the Executive Board of the same date. That's D1275. And those minutes reflect that on that date Mr. Karadzic submitted a report on the situation which was endorsed, and the decision to dissolve the Trebinje Municipal Board was adopted. A working group with Mr. Vucurevic named first was to be formed to conduct all affairs until new organs were constituted and that working group was obliged to consult with the Executive Board and Mr. Karadzic. Now, that's an accurate reflection of what happened with respect to Mr. Karadzic's involvement in the difficulties Mr. Vucurevic was having in Trebinje and his salvaging of the position of what he called my man Bozo Vucurevic as the leading figure in Trebinje; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I don't know whether he called him my man because he never called him so before me, but as to the fact that there were conflicts or perhaps better to say problems in the local organisation of Trebinje, that's correct. But it didn't happen only in Trebinje. It happened in other places, too. Many people saw themselves as leaders and party foremen, and in this competition there were occasional clashes of all sorts. However, as far as Trebinje specifically is concerned, it's true that Karadzic went there and he informed us of the situation, and it's also true that Mr. Rajko Dukic and I, he as president of the Executive Board and I as the secretary, went to attend that session of the Municipal Assembly in Trebinje where these problems were discussed, and after that session the problem was forestalled. Consultations took place, although not immediately, and the problem was solved not only in Trebinje but in other places too. It existed in other places, too, but Trebinje was the glaring example of problems and disunity in self-organisation, which is small wonder. Those were the first party elections and many people saw it as a chance to push their ambitions. That is how --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I appreciate that you're about to go into a good deal of detail about Trebinje. We have a good deal of information about that. I want to focus on other aspects of this same issue. As you point out, indeed this was not the only occasion that triggered the intervention of the SDS republic level authorities, and indeed it was not the first or last time that Mr. Karadzic ensured the composition of the local authorities by intervening in a similar manner. So, for example, in June of 1991, as we know from P2557, Mr. Karadzic had a conversation with locals from Prijedor and was alerted to problems that they were having, and that was a conversation with Mr. Goran Babic from Prijedor. Mr. Karadzic told Babic: "Tell those people who made problems that they cannot join the party now. That is my order." Page 3: "Tell them that I will introduce new measures in Prijedor and that I will tell them who the President will be there." "Tell him," referring to Mr. Srdic in that case, "everything. Tell him that I will dissolve board and I will place ten people to lead the party. Tell him that I forbid any one of them to get closer to the party. If you are not able to organise the real democratic elections without those bastards, I will name 10 to 15 people to lead it as I did last time." So P2557, an intercepted telephone conversation in June of 1991, reflects another occasion on which Mr. Karadzic monitored the situation in the municipality and intervened to ensure that the composition remained as the SDS republic level desired; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I really can't say anything about your assertion. I didn't take part in it. I did take part in the events in Trebinje, but as for anything else, I can't say anything because it doesn't concern me, and you don't find that in the statement either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you another event reflected in D1289. That's a conversation that took place a little earlier in June between Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Brdjanin, and Mr. Cvetkovic. And again Mr. Karadzic is complaining about any departures from the SDS republic level party line, and he states: "They are complete idiots. Insolent motherfuckers. As long as they are in SDS it will be decided here. What is like that in a global picture and what is not like that. Whoever will not accept this can fuck themselves and then we are going tell the people what they are doing. I will send them to hell. Those are idiots. This is the party policy and whoever wants to eat shit, they will have to take off the SDS badge and eat shit in their own name." That's at page 6. And he goes on on the next page of that intercepted telephone conversation to state: "If you ruin this, we will have --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither we nor the witness see the part of the intercept that Mr. Tieger is referring to. Could we have that on the screen so that the conversation is read out in interpretation, because it otherwise may have a changed meaning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that on the screen, the part you were referring to, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the first question -- this is a document in evidence that by the way was introduced by the Defence. The first question is the extent to which the witness has any familiarity at all with this event, and then the nuances of the translation, if any, may or may not be relevant. But I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be fair enough if you are going to quote a substantive part of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm now turning to page 7 of the English. That's -- where Mr. Karadzic stated: "If you ruin this, we will have new municipal elections, and I guarantee that none of you is going to be on the list. I will be making the list. I will come to Banja Luka for a month and make SDS to this." Mr. Komad, were you familiar with this and is this not a reflection yet again of Mr. Karadzic overseeing, monitoring, overseeing, and intervening to ensure that the SDS republic level party line was adhered to?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Given the fact that I'm not included in this conversation, I can't say anything about it. Knowing Mr. Karadzic as a man, I find it difficult to believe that he would use such language and vulgarity because I consider him to be a high-brow intellectual and a highly moral person. I did not participate in the conversation, so I wonder why this question is put to me. I couldn't have been present at every conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question is put to you, Mr. Komad, because you make certain assertions in your statement based ostensibly on your own experience. So I am testing whether those assertions are contrary to your experience or whether or not your experience is lacking in such a way that maybe the assertions you make are contradicted by facts about which you did not know or claim not to know. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I do understand, but you see I explained the situation in Trebinje. I described it briefly. I haven't touched upon anything else. I did say that there were problems, of course, and I still say that, because it was the very beginning of multi-party organisation and the beginning of the party as a political entity. Of course there were problems, and they were being dealt on the go. As far as I know, it was done on a democratic basis through constructive dialogue and raising important issues. That was the policy of the party, to deal with matters through dialogue, taking into account the general values that the party had built into its platform. That was the basis for such conversations and dialogue. And the same principle was supposed to be -- was supposed to have been followed in the field when organising its work in the municipalities and local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to dwell on this for long, but with respect to your comment about constructive dialogue and general values, let me ask you about some other evidence we've seen. P2556 is an intercepted telephone conversation with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Stevandic from January of 1992, and among other things in that conversation Mr. Karadzic says: "Well, I will not -- I will not -- well, let them go fuck themselves. Whoever makes a mistake, I will suspend him and throw him out of the party. I do not give a fuck. I will throw the shit heads out by a single stroke of the pen. I cross him. He is not in this party. As soon as he betrays the basic -- the basic flows of the party and the principal policy of the party." Those excerpts are found at pages 4 through 5.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have this text in the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was that a question, sir? I confirm that I did not take part in such conversations and I do not recognise Mr. Karadzic in this. I do not dispute that he was perhaps upset and agitated when people say things, but his general demeanour as party president did not boil down to what you are insisting on. Quite the other way around. We were always in favour of democratic principles and everything that was contained in the party programme and the programme of the main and Executive Boards. We were in favour of the party acting along the agreed principles, democratic principles. I can cite an example in favour of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've had an opportunity to cite examples before. I just wanted to -- I take it then that the positions reflected in this intercept were not part of the constructive dialogue that you referred to in your earlier answer; right?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Well, if that was -- I was discussing the party principles and not a single conversation, which may have been imbued with emotion or something else based on the reasons for it. I was discussing the principles of the party and the principles followed by party organs. Its president was also an organ of the party, so perhaps in affection he may have said something, but it was not the policy or standing practice applied by the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've already mentioned and we've discussed to some extent Mr. Vucurevic, who was the leading figure in Trebinje, the president of the SAO Herzegovina and the leading figure there, and this Chamber's already received evidence in D3170, that's a document tendered by the Defence, where Mr. Karadzic said to him: "Keep everything under your control, the entire Herzegovina." Now, Mr. Vucurevic in fact was someone who was close to and deferential to Mr. Karadzic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And on the other side of Bosnia, that is in the north-west part of Bosnia, was the Krajina, and Mr. Brdjanin is someone who regularly checked in with Mr. Karadzic for guidance, direction, and approval; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: It wasn't only Brdjanin. I think Vojo Kupresanin sought advice much more than he did, as well as some others from Krajina. However, Brdjanin was one of the group as I have stated in the statement. Now, if you're asking me who came to see him the most, then it was the men I mentioned, Vukic, Radic, Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the last two names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this includes Brdjanin. I really can't say who came to see him most frequently. If I try to think back, it seems to me that they all came to see him rather frequently. Brdjanin didn't come more often than the others, the others I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. We have received evidence, that is this Trial Chamber has received evidence of a particular telephone call that Mr. Brdjanin had with Mr. Karadzic on the 31st of October, 1991. That's P2549. Mr. Brdjanin calls concerning the problem with a dance that has been scheduled that he thinks was inappropriately scheduled, and Dr. Karadzic asks him: "Can't you solve a single problem without Karadzic?" "You have all the power in Krajina. Why don't you exercise this power?" And then he continues after Brdjanin tells him, well, someone -- pages 4 through 5 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask that the things being referred to be shown to us and to the witness especially. This is not the translation. It was simply Mr. Tieger's interpretation and we lose the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is not my interpretation. I'm reading from the English translation of a document that's in evidence. I don't -- since it is in evidence, I don't consider that for the purposes of this question it's necessary for the witness to follow. I'm happy if he can. I can call it up. And it is up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in order to elicit an informed answer, it would be fair to show the document to the witness. Let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And now moving on to page 5 of the English, as I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you can move the -- you can move it one more page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic tells him: "Come on, man, do your job. Don't call me about every minor problem. I am not your nanny. You have power in your hands, you have presidents of municipalities through whom you can exercise as power until we achieve autonomy. You should exercise power vigorously and to the fullest. Not a single bird should be allowed to fly over Krajina and there not be a shortage of men from Krajina for the army. You must establish all that. I've seen what was written and sent. All of that must be implemented. Take care of that. Call each and every municipality president and keep checking if it has been implemented and accomplished." Now, Mr. Komad, do you recall what was happening at this time and what Mr. Karadzic was referring to when he talked about the need to implement all that was written and sent; that is, when he spoke to Brdjanin about that on the 31st of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I can't say anything really with regard to your question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at P2548 then. This is a telex that's entitled "The Sarajevo SDS Order," and it refers to the meeting held on the 26th of October, 1991; that is, five days before the meeting we just looked at. A meeting that was chaired by Dr. Karadzic. And it orders, among other things, to form commands and institute permanent watch immediately, to institute full mobility of the territorial army, to form field units and name their substitutes, to take over power in public firms, post office, account-keeping institutions," that means the SVK, I take it, "administration of justice, and especially in mass communication media," and then it goes on to order other things. Mr. Komad, that's what Mr. Karadzic was directing Mr. Brdjanin to do in that October 31st conversation; correct? And that's what was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: What was the question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I asked you earlier if you knew what Mr. Karadzic was referring to when he was adamantly instructing Mr. Brdjanin what to do on the 31st of October. You said that you professed not to know. So I showed you now the SDS order of the 26th of October, from five days before, and I asked you if, in fact, that wasn't what was happening at the time and that was what Mr. Karadzic was referring to when he was talking to, at least in part, to Mr. Brdjanin on the 31st.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is a SAO Krajina document. Those were the issues discussed at that level in that body if this is indeed so. I had no possibility of being included in it all. As I've stated at the beginning, I'm here to testify to the work and functioning of the party organs and not the executive organs. The SAO Krajina was a type of the executive organ at this particular point in time. I cannot state any conclusions of mine regarding documents as this one and this type of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it's your testimony to this Chamber that you knew nothing about these events and what was happening at that time with respect to forming commands, taking over power in public firms and so on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I was not included in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at P958. P958 reflects a speech given by Mr. Karadzic before -- just before the plebiscite in November of 1991, and I'd like to look at certain aspects of that. At page 4 of the English and page 2 -- well, it's hard to say how this is in e-court. Page 2 of the text in B/C/S. It won't be e-court page 2 because we have a cover page as well and some other pages, but it will be the second page of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC STATES
utterances.text: "I'm kindly asking you, I've seen it not only in Krajina but also in Pale, you should seize completely and energetically. It cannot happen that a company manager is not loyal to the party where that party is in power. We cannot have a radio chairman or a newspaper editor who is not implementing the policy of the party in power." And then he continues in the next paragraph: "Be prepared soon to take over the SDK decisively, I mean to appoint your own man in the SDK." Now -- and the SDK is the account-keeping facility; correct, Mr. Komad?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then at page 10 of the English, and that's the third to last page of the text in B/C/S, Mr. Karadzic states: "You presidents of municipalities, you have to do this job. You and especially if the army instructs you to do it, no one else, no employee in charge. You and nobody else, because you are presidents of the national defence councils, and you are commanders of your towns. And also in Krajina, especially where the war is going on, everything that Brdjanin has written for you." Now, based on those two entries alone, Mr. Komad, this is a reflection of Dr. Karadzic telling municipality presidents and others gathered for the plebiscite speech about the need to implement the Sarajevo SDS order of the 26th of October, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: First of all, I can say that I was not in attendance when this speech was given. That's one thing. Another thing, when you read this out, I see that reference is made to the policy that had already been established at the national parties and ethnic divisions in the different municipalities and companies. Of course, the goal was to have the personnel chosen and to be clear on the ideology and platform chosen by the party. It was a lead-up to the war, in fact, and the will of the people was clear because people were fearful and there were conflicts in the environs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, threatening it with war. So the part that you quoted from Mr. Karadzic's speech, this is the first time I hear of it, but that is what it is stated, the ideology of the party that was supposed to be conveyed to where it was supposed to go, that is to say, to the people. As for the concept of this speech, I may have a separate opinion, but this is the first time I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, maybe you can tell us then, Mr. Komad, who Mr. Karadzic is referring to at page 5 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S text. And if we look at the first full paragraph in English which begins with Mr. Karadzic talking about "We and the Croats waking up in a state with the borders recognised by Europe," and then just before the italicised portion in English Mr. Karadzic states: "Trifko, can I have some water? Get that kid to bring it."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly read slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He's referring to you, isn't he, Mr. Komad?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: That may be. There are other Trifkos, but it could be me. I can't remember. And given the fact that I hear of this text for the first time, I simply stated my view on the general position presented therein, but I can't really read the original. It is so dense and illegible that I can't make things out. I think I've provided you with my position when I said that it was already the multi-party stage and the functioning of the parties. He was basically addressing the deputies of the SDS in the various municipalities and SDS personnel in different companies where they represented the party. I don't know whether this refers to me. It may well be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I note the time. I don't know if I've exhausted my time as allocated, but I don't think I have much more than ten minutes in any event, but I think it's better -- I can do it in a more efficient fashion I think if we take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll break, but before we do, about this document, in particular translation. I note there are several emphasis or italicisation. Who did that, while there's none in the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can check on that, Mr. President. This translation, so far as I'm aware, has appeared in various cases, so it wasn't done specifically for this case. It was inherited. But I'm happy to check and see if it's more suitable to eliminate the italics and replace it with normal font.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could do so. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, we're still discussing the plebiscite speech of November 1991. That's P986. And I wanted to turn you to a different excerpt, and that is found at page 6 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S. And there Mr. Karadzic says the following -- that paragraph begins with a discussion about what Mr. Karadzic says he told Izetbegovic concerning immigrants, Muslim immigrants from other areas to Bosnia, and he says: "But I am telling you whatever Bosnia we have one day, no Muslim foundation shall ever be laid in Serb areas and Serb villages whether or not you import Turks, because we will instruct Serbs not to sell land to Muslims. The first foundations that are laid will be blown up and all foundations that are laid will be blown up." And then he continues some sentences later: "They are implementing a demographic policy here, but we will be implementing one, too, and the whole world will understand that. The world will understand when we tell them that we will not allow the demographic picture to change either naturally or artificially. No way. Our territories are ours. We may be hungry, but we will be there." And then he continues: "You must not sell land to Muslims. You must not, because this is a fight to the finish, a battle for living space." Now, first of all, Mr. Komad, having heard these remarks, does that refresh your recollection about your attendance at the plebiscite speech in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither the interpreters nor the witness nor I saw this passage on the screen. We did not see that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have it at page 6 of the e-court at the bottom. That would be the one, two -- the third full page of text and the last paragraph of that page and continuing on to the top of page 7 of the e-court. Or page 4 of the full text if the witness wants to look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the reference for the B/C/S and have it displayed on the screen, the Serbian page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's P986. It's the one, two --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P986, the third page of text in B/C/S, the bottom paragraph beginning [B/C/S Spoken], et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's -- the "et cetera" is precisely what I want to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not disputing it. I'm just identifying where the passage is found.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I certainly want the witness to see that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we on the correct page, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President? I don't know what else I can do other than to call up the -- oh, I'm sorry. Okay. I see the problem. It's P958. My apologies to the registrar. Otherwise, everything applies. And as I say, the third -- I think it's page 6 of the B/C/S, but it's in any event the third page of text. That's it. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: See at that last paragraph, Mr. Komad? That's the portion that I was quoting --

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Very poorly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, just to recap quickly, it begins with a reference to the Muslim gentlemen establishing a ministry. It continues on about no Muslim foundations shall ever be laid in Serb areas. First foundations will be blown up, and then several sentences later: "They are implementing a demographic policy here. We will not allow the demographic picture to change either naturally or artificially." And then finally, I believe at the top of the next page, but I won't move any faster than you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And perhaps we can just show the next page in B/C/S and get rid of the English for the moment. No. We're going to have both pages at the same time, but that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally it states: "You must not sell land to Muslims, you must not, because this is a fight to the finish, a battle for living space."

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, I see what you're driving at. The question is am I aware of it or not. You keep asserting this and trying to portray Mr. Karadzic as an absolutist, a man who ruled absolutely without the involvement of any authorities, and I disagree about that. This is just a verbal expression of anger, anger about the situation that was already what it was on the ground. There was already mistreatment of Serbian people, displacements, movements of population. If there is any expression of anger, it was part of the dialogue and attempts to find solutions by pointing out to the problems that was the meaning. The party advocated this and Mr. Karadzic too. Let's go back to Trebinje where you said that Karadzic was an absolutist, and then I would like to ask how come he didn't deal with it? Why did Rajko Dukic and I have to go there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, I went through at that with you. I'm not going back there. I showed you the documents that are in evidence, the contemporaneous statements that were made at the time. So you had plenty of opportunity to do that. If Mr. Karadzic wants to take you back there, he's more than welcome to do so. Let's stick to what I'm talking about right now which is Mr. Karadzic's remarks in November about the demographic policy and the demographic picture and the battle for living space. And in that connection, I want to take you to paragraph 24 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: In November 1991, there were already movements of the Serbian population, especially from Croatia. there were convoys of refugees from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. This is not a debate. What I'm trying to do is ask questions to focus on certain areas, particularly certain areas that you've covered in your statement. I'm about to move to one of those paragraphs. So I'd appreciate it if you would listen to the questions and answer the question asked rather than making a speech about what you think the impact of your testimony so far has been or not been. In paragraph 24 of your statement, you refer to a meeting between Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Tudjman. And in connection with the demographic picture, I wanted to ask you about some aspects of that meeting which are not reflected in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if we could turn to P986, please, and this time it is P986.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: These, in fact, are the minutes of the meeting in January of 1992 between Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Tudjman, and other members of -- and other associates of Mr. Tudjman. At page 6 of the English and page -- well, the page that has the ERN 9181 in B/C/S. You will find those ERNs at the top of the page. Mr. Koljevic states: "An independent Bosnia does not suit us at all because it brings us and we think the Croatian people into a situation where we are separated from our motherlands." At page 13 of the English and at page 9189 of the -- in B/C/S, Mr. Koljevic states that it is not so impossible to divide Bosnia with the aim of homogeneity of certain areas. He says that everything is possible but complains that that option is excluded on the basis of a stand taken by the internationals in advance when they look at the leopard skin aspect of Bosnian demographics. And page 32 of the English and the page which is 9213 through 9214 of the B/C/S, Mr. Koljevic talks about delimiting territorial boundaries and arranging for the transfer of property and population, and he states the term "homogeneity" was, as you know, "vilified in Yugoslavia. Why should it be something terrible for people to live with people who are closest to them?" And Tudjman responds that: "Whenever national problems so conceived emerged as they did with us, that was resolved," and he refers to World War I and World War II, "that was brought to a conclusion by exchanges." So, Mr. Komad, the meeting between Koljevic and Tudjman which you referred to in paragraph 24 of your statement in fact reflected a further aspect of Bosnian Serb concerns about the demographic picture and a further reflection of their interest in ensuring that ethnic separation took place in a manner such that the -- the final demographic picture was suitable to the Bosnian Serbs. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I was present when Mr. Koljevic left for Zagreb and when he returned from Zagreb. I see this transcript for the first time, but I know his reaction, and I reflected it in my statement. He went on that trip to beg Tudjman and the leadership of Croatia to do everything within their influence to stop the winds of war from spilling from Croatia into Bosnia. That was the purpose of his visit. And to ask that all issues, including borders, to be resolved by dialogue. I remember well, and I know this well because I'm from Herzegovina, Tudjman said -- sorry. He said, "Do you want Herzegovina to be your border?" And Tudjman said, "Yes, on the condition that you move Muslims to your yard." And that explains the later coalition between Muslims and Croats. I did not see this transcript before, but I'm just relaying my impressions because I was present there, and that's what I said in my testimony. As for the other remarks on which you insist, of course I was not fully informed until the end, because transcript is one thing and my general impression that I stated is another.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, I have two hopefully quick matters. The first is, and it involves having you listen first to an intercept and then a brief portion of a video-tape. So if we can call up 65 ter 30304, please. Maybe we better start that again. Mr. Komad, this is a conversation between you and Mr. Milorad Bojovic on the 4th of October, 1991, and I just wanted to give you a chance to listen to it briefly. I won't play the entirety of it but you're welcome to look at the transcript of that conversation if you wish, but let's play portion of it first so you can presumably recognise yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's enough for now. The conversation will continue, Mr. Komad, and I can put up the two transcripts briefly for the benefit of the Court. This is a conversation between -- well, first of all, let me ask you quickly if you recognise your own voice and that of Mr. Bojovic?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I recognise my voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as you heard from the tape, this is a conversation in which you call because Professor Koljevic said that you should talk. You talk about the Crisis Staff and the staff for regionalisation. Mr. Bojovic says that he thought that they should not take any steps without an idea of how it should be done and what your plan is up there. You talk about the decisions of the government of SAO Herzegovina and SAO Krajina, et cetera, and Mr. Bojovic talks about the need for synchronisation, and the concluding part of the excerpt we heard thus today was Mr. Bojovic says that they called so they wouldn't do anything stupid or rash, and you say all preparations should be carried out. And he says, "Of course, that's why I'm asking you because nothing can be done without your approval." And you say, "Well, then, there you are." And he says he's asking because you -- because these people have not been informed of these matters, et cetera. So was that the -- let me ask you, was that the type of conversation you were having with municipality figures at that time in respect of the implementation of regionalisation and the decisions of SAOs?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes. If there were issues, yes. If there were such issues, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender 30304, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6248, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Komad, there was a brief discussion earlier about the language used by Mr. Karadzic, and I had the impression you were indicating some surprise at that, so I wanted to briefly play 65 ter -- or at least a portion of 65 ter 40136B, which takes place around the time we've been talking about; that is, around the time of the plebiscite in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't hear the sound.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] "Reporter: We no longer have any obligations towards the rest of Yugoslavia. We have the right to self-determination and the right for people to self-organise. When asked if it wouldn't be an act of unconstitutional destruction of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Karadzic replied in a not quite diplomatically. "Karadzic: You cannot fuck up the entire Yugoslavia expecting Bosnia to remain a virgin. No way! To point out at the end, three million ballot papers have gone out to polling stations, two millions for Serbs, the rest for the others. The balloting is reportedly also taking place in Serbia, America, wherever people live. "Many dilemmas have been raised by the colour of the ballot papers. The blue ones are for the Serbs, the yellow ones for the others. Many in Bosnia and Herzegovina noticed a similarity with the notorious yellow armbands. The SDS response for this was solely caused by technical difficulties."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Komad, as you can see, this deals with the subject matter that we discussed during the course of your testimony to some extent, but mainly I wanted to show it to you because of your reaction to some of the language you heard from Dr. Karadzic. Here we see

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC PUBLICLY SAYING
utterances.text: "You cannot fuck up the entire Yugoslavia expecting Bosnia to remain a virgin. No way!" as a public broadcast. Did you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it was a joke. Obviously it was not appropriate, but the then journalists such as that one were intent upon showing Karadzic and other Serbs as lacking in culture, lacking in education, and so on and so forth. I believe that this was why this was shown. This was not the way he normally communicated. I already told you that there was a lot of anger, but this is not a result of anger, but it was a joke which should not have been aired publicly. If it was uttered in a small crowd of people, it should have been appropriate. It would have been received as a joke. As far as I know him, that's not the way he spoke publicly. He must have been joking. As you can see from the context, it was more of a joke than the real thing or his real expression of a real opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this excerpt, Mr. President, and that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6249, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. Not much. I hope I will finish very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Komad, on page 41 of today's transcript Mr. Tieger summarised on line 13 and he said that you said that the Crisis Staff and the staff for regionalisation. Could you please make it clear, which of the two staffs existed? Did the two -- or did both exist in the autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the staff for regionalisation existed, i.e., it was either a board or a staff for regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time did we have a Crisis Staff at the party level?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: If you will allow me. In my conversation in the intercept, I use the term the Crisis Staff for regionalisation, and I would like to correct myself, and I did it on -- in the conversation as well, as you could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who else accompanied Professor Koljevic on behalf of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency to meet with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Boras, a member of the Presidency. The Croatian member of the Presidency. Franjo Boras I believe was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to those parts and elements where the import of population from Turkey is mentioned, do you know what that refers to? Did you know at that time what was going on?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: There was talk about the Mujahedin being on their way to Bosnia, that they had set up their camps where they prepared themselves. We had reports, but the information was not very specific. We did receive information, but it was not complete, but such information already reached us and circulated around Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sokolovic Kolonija is also mentioned. It was built in Serbian Ilidza. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what is meant when one says the changing of an ethnic composition, what operations?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I wanted to say before this Trial Chamber that the spiritual status of the Serbs when they were compared with the other two religious communities that existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina had to do with a long-term initiative that the Serbian being or the Serbian culture or the Serbian spiritual culture is being quashed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. By way of example, I can tell you that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the Second World War until the year 1990, only one church was built in Krajpolje where I was born, and there was a ban ongoing there. In contrast, over 1.000 religious edifices were built in Bosnia-Herzegovina serving Catholics and Muslims. Likewise, not a single letter, not for a single hour was Serbian Orthodox culture and thought in Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1945 to 1990. In contrast, there was an Islamic theological college which was in Bascarsija. It was set up in 1970 as the only one in Europe. Also, there is a Franciscan theology, Jesuit theology, and the secondary theological school in Visoko. During that period of time not a single letter was thought about the Serbian Orthodox culture. So there was a tendency to do away with the Serbian culture, and this information testifies to that. On the eve of the war I analysed the political postcards that were published in Bosnia-Herzegovina with a priest. You could not see any symbol of the Serbian spiritual or Orthodox culture in any of the postcards. In addition to that, settlements like you have just mentioned were built because various entities gathered around those places of worship.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that you said "tourist leaflets" on line 10 and it says "political."

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes. Those were touristic leaflets, not political leaflets. I must have misspoken.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P2548.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation for the fact that five days before the conversation with Brdjanin that you were shown that Brdjanin had said that there had been a meeting and that he was instructed to do the things that he mentioned? Can you look at the document? Can you tell the Trial Chamber what was applied in 1991, in October 1991? Did we set up garrison commands?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about that. I don't know that any of these things were implemented. I don't have any information to that effect. Take over power in public companies. We couldn't do that since the -- the authorities had already been set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we put a ban on issuing building permits?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we put a ban on the employment of people who came from the war-struck areas?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Paragraph 9, okay. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about 13? Did we impose higher tax rates in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
