utterances.text: The bullet point 3, did we form field units and name their substitutes?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All in all, would you say that that document arose from the party politics? Was it ever applied?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I've already told you when the Prosecutor was examining me that I don't think so. Not only do I not thing so, I'm sure that it wasn't a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 23 you discussed an intercept featuring myself and Mr. Bozo Vucurevic. A line was taken out of the context there, and in that line there is reference to control.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask for the document to be displayed. I believe that it is D3170. Can we go to the following page in Serbian, and I believe that we should be on the follow page in English as well. In English it's the last line on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please read the fourth line from the top.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: "Whatever they have, whatever companies they have and can get from you from the company, they all found it there from one company."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, is this about political control or is it about procurement and the functioning of the companies?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: It's about the functioning of the companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How were decisions made within the party?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I've already told you, but I repeat. The party tried to find the best democratic solutions that existed in Europe and in the world. By way of example, I would like to mention the political advisory body for ethnical co-operation which consisted of the three members of academy, the three top intellectuals from the Serbian culture. That council, that advisory body, had a major input on the decision-making process. They sought the most democratic solutions that could be applied at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Most commonly the party carried out activities in the field, and it was the fieldwork that impacted the decision-making process the most. It was not the leadership of the party but the municipalities that did that. It was a democratic procedure which would discuss issues like the statute, the programmes, some political positions with regard to the plebiscite, and things like that. All that was first checked in the field. We passed that by municipal bodies. We even carried out some sort of research, opinion surveys to hear what the people think, people in the field, at grassroot what they think, and that's how decisions were made. Everything that was decided was published by the party. We had our own bulletins. We had our own newsletter. Where we could not penetrate public media in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we issued our own bulletins. We published them on behalf of the party. The general public was present when it comes to all the pertinent issues that had to be defined by the party and that had to be launched by the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell the Trial Chamber who had the right to distort a decision that was democratically made? Who was in charge of the implementation of such decisions?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: The Executive Board was in charge of the implementation of decisions. I also participated in the Executive Board decisions of the Assemblies, the highest body of the party. They launched those decisions, and the Executive Board was tasked with the implementation of such decisions to make sure that those decisions were implemented among the people, among the basic cells of our party at the local level. That was the kind of policy that was pursued by the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anybody had the right to apply the programme of another party and pass it as the programme of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No. There was such attempts, but the answer's no. There were some elements from the old system, from the League of Communists, that tried to assert themselves, but what was positive was applied, but what the organs deemed not to be applicable could not be applied at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 21, there was reference to the disbanding of the Executive Board of the party in Trebinje. Is that something that was contrary to the statute or was that envisaged by the statute?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: The statute envisaged that, but the experience was still practically non-existent. It was a period when we were making our first step on the democratic path, and the -- an executive -- a Municipal Board could be disbanded if there were quarrels and if there were activities contrary to the basic principles, and in that sense one could reach a decision on the disbanding of a Municipal Board and the Executive Board of the party at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be instructed to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor imputed to me that I participated in the events in Trebinje --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes. Could you start again. Please be slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. I'll try. When it comes to the disbanding of Municipal Boards and the local bodies of authority, that was based on the statute. There was a provision in the statute to that effect, that such boards could be disbanded due to local disagreements, activities contrary to the statute and programme of the party. In that case the party could be disbanded. When it comes to Trebinje more specifically, because it was said to me that I can say what I think, if you, Mr. President, had absolute power, I can ask you why didn't you do that when you were in Trebinje for two days? It was the Executive Board that concluded that Rajko Dukic, the President of the Executive Board, and I, as the secretary, should go to Trebinje in order to resolve the situation there. That procedure is certainly democratic because we sought the best solutions in order to deal with the situation in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the intercepts involving Kozic and Vucurevic, Kominic [phoen] is mentioned as well as the SPO. Could you tell the Trial Chamber who those people were? What were those bodies, and what was the attitude of that party towards the SDS with regard to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down and not to start his answer before the question is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please wait a bit or put a pause before you start answering the question, and please speak very slowly. Could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SPO was a political organisation based in Belgrade and led by Vuk Draskovic. At that period of multi-party activity, the SPO had established its branch or its organisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina with a focus on the Serb inhabited areas. The SPO in a way competed with the SDS. They used many means to push out the SDS from those parts of the country where we had already set up municipal bodies. As for the names, can you remind me of the last name?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Kominic?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: He was the deputy, I believe. Anyway, he was from the top of Vuk Draskovic's party in Belgrade. He was literally critic active in Belgrade and who came to Trebinje with the purpose of expanding the activity of his party in competition with the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber what was the position, especially vis-a-vis extremism of the SDS and the SPO?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: The SPO was a more radical organisation in terms of their position concerning the activities of Serbs through the political system than was the case with the SDS. Generally speaking, the SDS had a moderate or more moderate policy which could already be by the time observed through the different documents and platform it published.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 20 and 21 there was discussion about Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 65 ter 30239.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were quoted from some documents from the beginning of the crisis. Some documents from early September were quoted to you. This one is the 17th of September. Please look at the third line from the bottom. What does Mr. Dukic say?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Do you want me to read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please just tell us what it's about. And the last part which says: "Trifko is kept abreast..."

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, Dukic is conveying his impressions from Trebinje. And he delegated that authority to inform me -- to inform you to tell us how we participated at the Municipal Assembly session in Trebinje. That was the purpose of this conversation as far as I can see. Of course we said that we were hoping that things would settle down there after our visit, and indeed it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And there it is stated that you were in favour of lifting the suspension from Grubac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that both Vucurevic and Grubac stay there. That was your proposal?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. Just put a pause. The interpreters are not able to follow up with your speed. Shall we start again, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at the Assembly session at Trebinje, I advocated or actually proposed that Vucurevic and Grubac should sit down as the two opposing parties as well as their associates in order to reach an agreement in those areas that were open to discussion rather than to have Grubac suspended. There were some proposals along that line. That was my proposal, which was accepted, at least at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said at the Assembly session, did you mean the Municipal Assembly session or the meeting of the party?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll read out what I say: "I proposed it to them back then but they didn't accept it. They did not accept it the first time round, and the Executive Board then reached a decision to suspend -- or, rather, to dissolve the Municipal Board." Was it the Municipal Board who made that decision or was it me?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: The municipal -- the Executive Board, Mr. President, as we can see from the conversation, and I know it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Two lines down I say again: "Well, yes, this can be done democratically in public forums," and then Lukic says that you spoke to Vucurevic. Now, help us out here. Dusko Kornjaca from Ljubina, is this a mistake?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President. Dusko Kornjaca, as far as I know, is from Cajnice, and Dusko Kozic is from Trebinje if that's the person in question. But I don't know why Dusko figures in this transcript in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we propose that Grubac remain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The third line from the top. My last sentence. Grubac's aims may be noble and good, but the means he chose are violent. Do you know what I advocated actually, what kind of instruments to be used in political life?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Always I've said already, you were exclusively for dialogue, for discussion to apply the best possible solutions that will suit the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next large remark of mine, the means and ways he applies are rough. One needs to take into account the model and method of the SDS rather than certain Communist or SPO principles or God knows what. We have our moderate democratic methods. And then further down we say the democratic -- a democratic party does not make decisions only but comes up with solutions. How does this tally with what you know about the party you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, you were fast again. Could you start again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Pardon. My entire testimony is to the effect that we were constantly looking for the best and most democratic solutions. We consulted the international community and scientists who could help us organise the work of the party. Now, as for how successful we were, that's a different matter. These were turbulent times with many difficulties of things we had inherited and the problems that were brought about by the looming conflict. This problem of things we inherited from the previous system that we had lived in before as well as the looming problems made things that much more difficult in applying the democratic principles of the SDS. If I were to make a summary of our activity, I would say that the party did not have any militant or any kind of absolutist methods. It was in constant search of the best methods. I've already mentioned what kind of bodies and people helped us who were active in our area and within our organisation. It was all done to create such methods. I mentioned that I was a member of the political council throughout its operation. It comprised the best intellectuals who had a great impact on our programme and activities as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown part of the transcript between Professor Koljevic and Franjo Boras with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P986.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you can help us out. Let's see if the document contains what you've mentioned was your impression?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not tendering this intercept?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then you should have confirmed with the witness whether the witness really spoke with you. I think he appears up to this page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In this document he does appear. We can leaf through it. We can keep going through it. Dukic mentions you on page 1.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As someone who worked on it?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 4 and 5, the witness spoke to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have that shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You actually scheduled some interviews on my behalf and I accepted it. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that. It was towards the bottom where it says: "Trifko has something else to ask you." Rajko said that. And then I asked you about that. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you the Trifko?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In this document, page 7 in the Serbian and 6 in the English, please. In this P986, which is on the screen. Page 7 in the Serbian, page 6 in the English version. The intercept transcript could be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, perhaps we should look at the previous page so as to see that it is Professor Koljevic who speaks. Look at the last long paragraph. "We essentially proposed a tripartite community." Can you look at it and tell us whether that is the gist of what was conveyed to you?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Please put it back, the paragraph, the one referred to by the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is Koljevic's intervention?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Once again Mr. Karadzic is not being mindful of the distinction between cross and examination-in-chief or redirect examination, so he's lapsing into a leading mode. He'll need to find out. And I think the witness has basically identified what he remembers of the information he received from Mr. Koljevic, but in any event, this would not be the way to proceed in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Komad, what Mr. Tieger presented as the topic and the gist of that meeting and what you know about it, does it accurately reflect what the meeting was about? What did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: As I've said already, I recall Mr. Koljevic going there and what his intentions were when he went to talk to Franjo Tudjman. I also paraphrased the words of the late Mr. Koljevic as to what he said upon his return. He told us, of course, that he had discussions and that he had conveyed -- he actually conveyed to us the thoughts of Mr. Tudjman as to the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina and some other parts. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the last paragraph, please, and tell us how does it tally with what you learned from Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, I mean that's an insistence - as we've seen before - a stubborn insistence by Dr. Karadzic on ignoring both the objection and the ruling by the Court. If Dr. Karadzic wants to ask generally about certain aspects in a non-leading way he can do so, but instead he offers up a -- he elicits a generalised account and then he goes right to the leading portions of the examination. So he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In your opinion, what the problem with the last question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He can certainly -- if he's moving on to a particular subject matter generally, then he can ask whether the witness was -- recalls any discussion about certain topics, but now he wants an affirmation of what's in the transcript, and the witness -- by now the witness has been reading from the transcript in any event as it stayed in front of him during the course of these questions. But I think it's very clear what Dr. Karadzic is trying to do here: He wants to pop this document in front of the witness and get affirmations about specific aspects of the document, and that is quite different than eliciting from the witness in a non-leading way what the witness was aware was addressed by Dr. Koljevic upon -- either before he went or upon his return.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Robinson, if you could assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think once Dr. Karadzic has shown that the witness is familiar with the context he's entitled to put -- to draw witness's attention to particular portions of the document and put a non-leading question to the witness, like how does that tally with your understanding. I don't think there's anything wrong with doing that or anything leading, and I think the Prosecution did that continuously during its case once it had established that a witness was familiar with the topic. It directed their attention to particular portions of documents or intercepts, and I don't think that this in any way is a leading way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That was my point of question for you, Mr. Tieger. Yes. You have some --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I won't argue it further so we can move forward in any event, but let me just say as a general matter: It's -- it's one thing to ask about a subject and then follow it up with a question. It's another thing to take a generalised topic -- "Were you ever" -- for example, "Were you ever in Sarajevo?" "Yes, you were." "Oh, you know where it is." And then here's a document about something specific. And that latter approach more closely resembles what we see Dr. Karadzic doing repeatedly here than a follow-up to more specific inquiries. As I say, I raise that as a general response to Mr. Robinson's point, but as for this particular ruling, I leave it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed. We'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Perhaps I can reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Koljevic go to see Tudjman in order to negotiate an aggressive or a democratic way to resolve the crisis?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: As I said already, the basic idea of Mr. Koljevic's trip to Zagreb was not to have the war spill over into Bosnia-Herzegovina, rather, to stop all war activity in Bosnia-Herzegovina to the extent possible and also in Croatia, because the war had already started there. So the specific goal of the trip to Zagreb was to invest an effort in stopping the war which was already at the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to the next page. Would you look at this and tell us -- the English page should remain the same. Could you tell us how this fits in? What is Professor Koljevic advocating?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: He's advocating any other alternative, including division, absolutely anything, any solution that is not war. So he is in favour of finding solutions for delimitation, agreements, negotiations. That was the purpose and his intention behind going to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we see English page 7 and Serbian page 9. In paragraph 3, Professor Koljevic says: "We had no wish to impose on the Muslim people any of our own options." Is Professor Koljevic telling the truth here?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we see Serbian page 11, English 8. I will read out to you the third paragraph by Koljevic: "We tried to offer a surplus of sovereignty instead of denying sovereignty. Let it be a Muslim sovereign, Serbian sovereign, and Croat sovereign Bosnia. Let it be a sovereign state of sovereign peoples." And then towards the bottom you see along the principles of Switzerland. What did you know about this position of Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: This position expressed by Professor Koljevic who was by the way also chairman of the political council of the Serbian Democratic Party, is a position that the Serbian Democratic Party and Professor Koljevic advocated in talks and in dialogue, including here with Gojko Susak. Those were the basic premises from which we proceeded in the party. We fought for the sovereignty not only of the Serbian people but of all peoples.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please, both in English and in Serbian. Serbian 12, English 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was partially quoted to you where Professor Koljevic says in view of the intermingled nature of territories, there would be the possibility of transfers and exchange in a civilised way, and then he says: "And this is already happening spontaneously. The ethnic, territorial, and demographic principles should be equally applied." Did anyone from the Serbian Democratic Party or any of its representatives in the government propose any violent, forced changes in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I understood you well, Mr. President. I do not know of any such ideas, if they existed at all in anyone's head, but certainly in the minds of the Serbian Democratic Party, members, and its representatives, there was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you together with me take part in my contacts with the grassroot level, and were you aware of what I recommended to our officials on the ground regarding co-existence with others, especially Muslims, in terms of atmosphere and relations?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: You advocated co-existence, living shoulder to shoulder wherever possible. If that was not possible, if the relations had been disrupted to that extent, you were in favour of division but on an equal footing. You were in favour for equal rights for every individual but also peoples as a whole. That was your principle and the principle of the party that you represented. I did not attend any meeting or any negotiations apart from some minor excesses where you would officially proceed from the position of hegemonism and lack of respect for other peoples. You put everyone on an equal footing, the Serbian people and all the other peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the policy and the strategy of the party you represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to call 1D05745 in e-court, please. 28 September 1991, talks between Trifko Komad, Branko Simic, and Radovan Karadzic. There is no other person with the same name and surname as you, right, Trifko Komad?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, you are introducing to go me Branko Simic from Mostar. And further down below Simic speaks to me. I'm reading this in English: [In English] "And there were disruptions in Opusici and Lokve, but I -- there isn't any serious problem there and the people are going back there and of course Muslims have all gone back." [Interpretation] I say, "uh-huh, uh-huh." Then Branko Simic: [In English] "Over there in the village of Opusici, Muslims and Serbs got together," [interpretation] I confirm [In English] "and are roasting lambs on the spit together."

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Lamb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then I say: "Excellent. Let it be. Let them know that we have nothing against them." And then further below: "One needs to keep repeating our forces, our weapons are against Ustasha. Do not join the Ustasha and you have nothing to fear." Do you recall this, and how does this position of mine fit in with your recollection of our position towards the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Precisely as you stated it, Mr. President. You always advocated that wherever possible normal relations should be established and fostered. You found examples for our common history of living together and working together, and you always advocated for all the positive vibrations and positive experience to be built into our relations, the relations between Serbs and Muslims and Croats in our multi-ethnic community in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Csn this document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3204, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 18 you were asked the question in which it is not clear, because negatives are used differently in our language and in English. The question was: "Do you claim, Mr. Komad, that despite the fact [In English] that fact again one of that extended meeting -- at the extended meeting of the deputies -- deputies club was aware of the variant A and B, and you were not aware of it?" [Interpretation] Then you answered: "No." Did you mean that you didn't know or that you don't claim that? It's a linguistic problem.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I meant to say that I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then in English the proper answer would be, "Yes, I claim that."

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, I claim that I was not aware of that, that I did not attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was discussion on pages 13 and 14 about the yellow ballot papers for the plebiscite of the Serbian people. Could you first tell us who was that journalist who prompted me to make that unsavory joke? Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: He was very well known, Smiljko Sagolj, a journalist of Croatian provenance who was notorious for many incidents and excesses as a journalist and his tendentious reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Smiljko Sagolj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he's regretting -- he's moaning about Bosnia, not Yugoslavia. How did you understand his comment? Why did I make that joke?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: The coalition was already there. The flags were already tied together, the chequerboard flag and the lilies flag. They were tied together in many public places and they were hoisted together as a sign of their coalition. The Croats had already made a pact with the Muslim side to make a coalition and to build an independent and sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the provocation he made and you reacted. I understood what you said as a joke, because I repeat I did not know you as that kind of person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you tell us about these different colours of ballot papers, especially the yellow ones, because you saw back there that Sagolj says we claimed it was for technical reasons?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, it was for technical reasons, because when counting we wanted to know how many members of other ethnic communities accepted our idea of living in a common state. If the Court allows me, I would like to make a small digression. If we were to analyse the programmes and the documents of the Serbian Democratic Party, the HDZ, and the SDA, if we were to make a sociological analysis, we would see that in our platforms all of us advocated democratic principles and those programmes coincide a great deal, especially in enactments. We differ mainly on one issue: In what kind of state we are going to live in. That was where the disagreement was. HDZ and the SDA wanted the principle of the majority to rule. They wanted to out-vote others, to out-vote us and marginalise us. So through these yellow ballot papers, we wanted to see how many members of other ethnic communities agree with the idea of living together in a common state. We were just testing the ground. That was our aim, not what Sagolj and some others suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that yellow colour of the ballot paper have a special meaning or connotation? Why was it yellow and not something else?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No matter what colour it was, they would always find something to object about. I know that yellow was chosen randomly so that we, the technical services, could more easily analyse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we now see 65 ter 31994. And you, of course, know who Miodrag Simovic is?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who is Miodrag Simovic? Can you tell the Court?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Miodrag Simovic is a professor at the law school of the university. He was deputy prime minister during the multi-party government. He was the deputy prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a candidate of the Serbian Democratic Party. He is now teaching at the university in Sarajevo, and he's also a member of the academy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before we upload this document, yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. Well, I'm having a hard time seeing how this won't run afoul of the general principle that I discussed. I mean, if Dr. Karadzic had said do you remember that I told Mr. Simovic or Mr. Simovic told me, that would clearly be a leading question. I don't know where we're heading here, but it seems to be potentially the same problem, because I don't know exactly offhand what the text of this intercept is about. It's difficult for me to speculate about. It's a relationship to something that was just raised, but it doesn't seem like this is going to work without being leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the topic was the colour of the ballot papers, and it is clarified in this intercept, but I wanted the Chamber to know who Miodrag Simovic was, what his importance and his position was, but I didn't want to say it myself. I wanted to elicit it from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let us see. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we get the next page, Serbian 2, English 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll read out towards the bottom. Karadzic says: "Uh-huh. And tell me about some of our other neighbours. Some of them are interested. Others are afraid of the plebiscite. Is that your impression too?" And Simovic says: "I believe many more people of other ethnicities will turn out at the referendum --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "-- than we can guess at this moment."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbian next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then he goes on: "That's what I think from some of my impressions from my contacts with him. That's my impression. You see, after all it's a great thing when we say Yugoslavia, declaring oneself in favour of Yugoslavia. They know it all." And he goes on to say that 90 per cent of them know that without Yugoslavia there is nothing. And then on the next page he says: "Although yesterday in 'Oslobodjenje' in some report he repeated it, saying that the colour yellow denotes a second-rate people, second-rate citizens, and I say he is a complete fool. I say he's a complete fool. We wanted the colour to be white. The printing press said they had no yellow paper and white was -- sorry, they had no white paper and yellow was cheaper anyway. And then I say again, he's an utter fool." So were we trying to send a message using that colour? Did we try to humiliate anyone?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No. No, we had no such intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning the election of the secretary, it was interpreted or translated that I was not nominated to become president of the party. Is nomination and election the same thing or are they two different things?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: They are two different things. You can be nominated by somebody, whereas election means that one is elected either by all citizens or by a certain circle defined by a document. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a difference between nomination and appointment? The secretary of the Executive Board as a neutral body, does he vote for one or the other faction or does he keep his neutrality?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: As I've already told you, the election or appointment is a more democratic form than nomination because it arises from the opinions and the decisions of a majority, the majority that is eligible to vote, whereas anybody can be nominated even by an individual. I already explained that I as the secretary was appointed based on the advertised opening and by virtue of my position I was a member of the Executive Board. I was not nominated. I was elected. A nomination is less democratic than appointment based on the advertised opening for a position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two more minutes, one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were shown some sentences from which it stems that everybody listened to me, that I was an autocrat, especially when it came to Krajina. Can you tell the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, please. I'm quite certain that I didn't use that term. This is commentary and leading at the same time and needs to be avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely. The Chamber agrees with Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I apologise. I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The picture that Mr. Tieger represented about me as a --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why doesn't Mr. Karadzic simply go to the specific reference or to the subject matter without trying to characterise it or comment on it in any way? It would seem to me to be much simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you need a break, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will finish before the break. It's very difficult, though, because Mr. Tieger made such a salad of his questions, so he showed so many documents that portrayed me in quite a different way, and now I would like to ask Mr. Komad what he knew about my relationship with people in the field, especially with the leaders in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have already spoke about your behaviour and conduct, about how you interacted with people as president. I showed as much as I could that you used all the possible democratic principles that could be applied in all of your activities, including what you did in Krajina. So I can't say anything else. I can't present any other of your traits than the ones that I did. In my written statement it says that your tolerance sometimes went beyond what could be expected resulting in a lack of consistency. When I was talking about activities as a president, I said that the meetings of the main boards were attended by people who had not been invited to attend them, but you believe that everybody had the right to have their say, that everybody had to be given the possibility to say what they wanted to say. I would like to confirm that when it comes to your attitude towards Krajina and the issues there, you sought democratic solutions that would be applied across the board including Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On line 23 you said "a lack of systematic nature" and it was recorded as "inconsistency."

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I would like this to be translated as the lack of systemic nature because at meetings you would set -- you would refrain from setting up the agenda. You left it to the others to do that. Sometimes you would even didn't -- would not do that. It was not very practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My last question: Did the Krajina leaders listen to me? What was their attitude towards me? Did anybody listen to me, especially those people from Krajina?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I believe that a majority respected you, that they showed respect, and as a result of that they agreed with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they obey me blindly?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: No, no. There were dialogues. I don't want to say that there were arguments. There were dialogues which were sometimes heated, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did somebody have to pay the price for disobeying me or contradicting me?

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: I don't know of any such examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am not going to call up a document which has already been admitted, which is P2552. Thank you, Mr. Komad. Thank you for the co-operation that I had with you over the years, and thank you for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: TRIFKO KOMAD
utterances.text: Thank you as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Komad. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go. But before we rise for a break, there are a couple of housekeeping matters I'd like to deal with now. The first is scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pursuant to the courtroom schedule on the intranet, it is noted as we are sitting for three days in the week of 20th of May, but given that Monday is a UN holiday, Whit Monday, we will be sitting on Friday as well, that is 24th of May, unless it would cause a lot of problems with the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me simply say, Mr. President, that when we consume UN holidays or for -- and add them to the schedules, it's much more difficult for the parties, I believe, because the services are quite different. So apart from the fact that it prevents hard working personnel - and everyone is working extremely hard - from getting what I would think is a much deserved break, it also becomes much more difficult to cope with preparation during that period because so much of the staff is otherwise gone, and I suspect that is replicated on the Defence side as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see the point, but it has been our practice, hasn't it, that while we are sitting four days a week when there's a holiday, we still continue to sit four days a week even if there's a holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It has been our practice, which is why I was able to make the comments I did on the basis of experience, and as I say, I suspect it would be echoed by the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we would prefer -- we've already scheduled all our witnesses for May, and we would have to now round up two more, which we'll do it if you order us to, but it's -- the information that we -- that coming from the Chamber, and the registry is not always very clear to us. For example, we thought we weren't signature on this Friday for a long time, and nobody notified us until a calendar popped up and all of a sudden we were sitting on this Friday, so we scrambled and we have enough witnesses for this week, but when we saw the calendar for May there were two weeks in which we only had three-day weeks, and so we scheduled the witnesses accordingly and it makes it difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We have three-day week in the week of 6th of May, but there seems to have been a mistake as regards the week of 20th May, but I will -- the Chamber will consider the issue, but you have problem with sitting on Friday, 24th of May specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we don't have a problem with that other than we would have to recruit some more witnesses for that period, and I don't know -- I think there's enough time between now and then we can probably do that. So we don't have a problem specifically with that date, but it makes it difficult for us when we get conflicting information about the calendar. So had we had the information originally when we filed -- when we prepared for May, we would have had no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will come back to this issue in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From my point of view as a person of a certain age, I was hoping for some more breaks. This rhythm is killing us all. We are working very hard. Our witnesses follow in a very rapid succession. I'm not complaining. I'm just trying to make sure that the Trial Chamber has that in mind. We all have to stay healthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. The final matter is related to the exhibit issue. The Chamber recalls that on the 20th of March, 2013, it requested that CLSS provide a revised translation for a specific excerpt of the video admitted into evidence as Exhibit P2 -- I'm sorry, P6211. The Chamber has now received a revised transcript in B/C/S as well as the corresponding English translation of this excerpt, and although there are only slight differences, the Chamber finds it preferable to have the revised versions in e-court. Accordingly, the Chamber instructs the Prosecution to upload the revised versions of the B/C/S transcript and English translation as provided by CLSS to replace those documents currently in e-court. We will resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, Judge Lattanzi cannot be with us for this session due to her official function. Yes. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelica. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Like everyone who speaks Serbian, I have to ask you and to remind myself to speak slowly and especially to make a pause between question questions and answers. Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I call up in e-court 1D7980. Please look at the screen. Do you see your statement on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, now I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see the last page so that the witness may identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you have said? Are there any errors? Are there any corrections needed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. It is a faithful reflection of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have your statement before you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well I shall ask for the leave of the Trial Chamber if you need to use it. If I were to ask you the same questions today as you were asked when this statement was taken, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellency, I tender this 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just note the revised statement has been filed, but I haven't had the time to check what the differences are. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There have been several paragraphs added to the revised -- to the original statement which deal with adjudicated facts and some additional documents which are referenced in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just checked paragraph 23. In my version I already have paras 60 to 82. But reference to 1D7305 has disappeared in the new para-23.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's actually in paragraph 59 now, and I think it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fifty-nine, yes. It was my mistake. I thought it was para 23. Yes, 59. It remains there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it was actually listed as an additional exhibit because it wasn't listed at the time we submitted this list and we have taken a position to put all untranslated documents as additional exhibits pursuant to the Trial Chamber's instruction, but we have in the meantime received a translation, so if the Chamber would be willing to consider it as an associated exhibit, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember you rose before I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I did rise just to tell you that there were 25 associated exhibits being offered and eight of them are not on our 65 ter list and we would ask that those eight be added to our 65 ter list mostly because they were received after the list was submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I hear from you, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Thank you. Yes, as we indicated in our e-mail yesterday evening, there have been 23 new paragraphs added to the statement, paragraphs 60 through 82. They reference a total of 17 new documents not mentioned anywhere else in the statement. Clearly this goes beyond the minor corrections and clarifications permitted at this stage under Rule 92 ter, so in our submission these additional paragraphs should be led live. I note Mr. Robinson's comments a moment ago that there is now a translation for 65 ter 1D07305. As far as I'm aware, we have not yet received that, so I had also objected to the admission of that document and paragraph 59 which is essentially devoted to a discussion of that document. If I can see the translation, I'd be happy to reconsider whether that objection still stands or not, but until I can see the English, that's difficult for me to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think there would be any problem for the Defence to lead live about 1D7305. Do you have any observation to make as regards the recently added paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We offered to the Prosecution to postpone the cross-examination of this witness so that they can have enough time to digest that material, and they've told us that they have enough time to digest the material and go ahead with the cross-examination now, but in line with the Chamber's practice they were requesting it be led live. If I'm misquoting Ms. Gustafson, she can tell me that, but that was my understanding of their position. But our position is that this is Dr. Karadzic's contribution and the only time he can make the contribution to his evidence, and we think that any remedy ought to be to have the Prosecution have as much time as they need for cross-examination. If you want to lead the evidence live as long as it's not charged against our time, we have no problem and we're not prejudiced by that, but we would be prejudiced if we would have to spend against the 300 hours that we're given for our whole case to lead evidence that can simply be postponed so that the Prosecution has enough time, and that's we think a more valuable use of the Chamber's time and a better remedy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I can just comment on one remark Mr. Robinson just made, which is that this is Dr. Karadzic's contribution and the only time he can make the contribution. In this case, the bulk of these additional paragraphs are the witness's comments on a number of documents that were shown to him, and I see no reason why if Dr. Karadzic knows he wants to do this he can't communicate sufficiently with his Defence team to ensure that this is done well in advance so we are not faced with this kind of -- this bulky new material at the last minute. And just in terms of the practice, it has been the Chamber's consistent practice when this kind of volume is added at the last minute of new material that this is led live and I believe there's a good reason for that. We are in this instance able to absorb this material into our preparations and we don't need a delay, but if there is no counter-balance in terms of some impact on the Defence's time, then in our view there will be no limit as to the amount of additional information that will appear in these 92 ter statements, and it will become a significant problem in terms of our preparation. It is not a simple matter to 24 hours prior to a cross-examination absorb and deal with this amount of new material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And your argument is that the minor changes that is to be covered by the so-called 48-hours rule is limited to really minor things so that these cannot be said to be minor changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Without repeating too much, I don't think we could really live with that kind of rule given that this is Dr. Karadzic's only opportunity to have input, and if he's relegated to a minor player in his own trial, I don't think that that's fair. Also, Mr. President, in terms of remedies for whatever let's say violations there might be, the Prosecution had many disclosure violations for which there were no remedies. So if you use the same logic that Ms. Gustafson has used, there would have been remedies for those violations to make sure that they didn't occur again, but also when you did give us six or eight weeks to deal with late disclosure, you didn't deduct that from the Prosecution's 300 hours. So it would be similar if you were to give -- make us lead this evidence live. You shouldn't deduct it from our 300 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One more question for clarification. You said that the Prosecution said to you that it is -- it would be okay to go ahead with cross-examination. Could you expand? Or whether Ms. Gustafson could clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's just that we don't need any additional time to prepare for this new material, just our position is it should be led live. And just in response to Mr. Robinson's remarks about past disclosure violations, this is the practice the Chamber applied to the Prosecution [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question. Even if the Chamber is to decide to admit these paras, you are not asking for additional time for the preparation of your cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the circumstances, i.e., given that the added material is not that much and that the Prosecution is ready to proceed with her cross-examination, we'll admit the statement but not the document whose 65 ter number is 1D7305. That paragraph should be led live. We'll give the number for the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit D3206, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And just I forgot to raise this: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber had an opportunity to skim through the statement. Para 44, the Chamber -- we will keep the first and last sentence, but the other part should be redacted, as well as paragraph 45, 47, and paragraph 49 to 51. They do contain too much detailed evidence, including names, ages of victims on crimes against Bosnian Serbs that are not relevant or necessary. With that caveat we admit this statement, and the other associated exhibits will be admitted and will be given numbers in due course by the registrar. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In light of Your Honour's ruling admitting these 23 additional paragraphs, unless there's been a recent change, there are no translations for 65 ter 1D07974 referenced at paragraph 81 or 65 ter 05392 referenced at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it the document that is being tendered? I forgot to mention that whether there's an English translation of 1D14014, which is referred to in para 38. Where do you find that document, Ms. Gustafson, 7974?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's referenced at paragraph 81 and 65 ter 05392 referenced at paragraph 79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it was listed as additional document and as such I take it, Mr. Karadzic, you're going to lead -- deal with it live.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, and also we do have a translation of 1014 that I can see in e-court, so I don't know if that's a problem with e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't have the time to look at it. If Mr. Karadzic could lead it live as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out in English the summary of Mr. Bjelica's statement, and then I will deal with the documents that need to be led live. [In English] Milovan Bjelica was born on 19th of October 1958 in Rogatica, Bosnia and Herzegovina. He now permanently resides in Sokolac municipality. Milovan Bjelica was a member of the SDS in the Sokolac municipality. He held several positions. First, in 1990, he was a member of the Sokolac Assembly. Later, in May 1991, Mr. Bjelica was elected as vice-president of the SDS Municipal Board. On 13th of January, 1992, he became president of the SDS Municipal Board in Sokolac. He was also a member of the SAO Romanija Assembly. The SDS was formed during 1990 following the formation of the SDS -- SDA and HDZ. In July that year, the founding assembly of the SDS was held in Sarajevo. The party's key objectives were to preserve Yugoslavia and the equality of the Serbian people in B and H. The most important organ of the SDS was the Main Board, and the Assembly which was -- among other things elected president of the party and implemented decisions of the SDS Assembly. Following the declaration of sovereignty of BH on 15th of November -- October 1991, it resulted in the breakdown of co-operation that had been established following the inter-party elections 1990. On 21st of November, 1991, the Serbs in BH adopted a decision to verify the proclaimed Serbian autonomous regions and later that year the reserve police force, Territorial Defence, and some reserve forces of the JNA that were mobilised due to the mounting political tensions. Muslim forces began to establish paramilitary groups, and by January 1992, the Patriotic League was fully formed. There were sabotage and terrorist attacks carried out by the Muslim units. There was also information that Muslims were volunteering fight in Croatia against the Serbs and bringing home weapons which alarmed the Serbian population. On April the 4th, 1992, the Rump Presidency of BH, which did not include the participation of the two Serbian representatives, declared a general mobilisation of its police, military, and paramilitary units. The Crisis Staff Sokolac municipality was formed in early April 1992. The Crisis Staff was independent in its work and received no instructions from the Presidency and National Assembly of Republika Srpska. There was no obligation to send documents of the Crisis Staff to those organs of the Republika Srpska. The Crisis Staffs were -- that were formed in municipalities and local communities were not a secret system of command and control. The Crisis Staff in Sokolac functioned in a democratic manner and helped with normal work and life in the municipality. A meeting of the Crisis Staff was held on 23rd of April that called for the maintenance of good ethnic relations and a return to normal life. SDA members refused to attend the meeting. Although the Crisis Staff called on the Muslim people for tolerance and co-existence, they started leaving the Sokolac settlements and all settlements where they were a minority population they left. There was no pressure of the authorities for them to leave, and some remained at their homes nearly until the end of the war. Those who remained lived in peace and were not abused. In the summer of 1992, as the member -- as the number of killed and wounded of Serbian Army, police, and civilians increased, the VRS called on civilians to hand over their weapons. Muslim units did not respond to that call and sabotage and terror continued. The already difficult situation in Sokolac increased when large numbers of Serbian refugees started to arrive. In summer of 1992 a number of incidents occurred in which Serbian civilians were killed by Muslim extremists. The VRS 2nd Romanija Brigade decided to demilitarise the area and Muslim units put up armed resistance. Casualties were sustained on both sides. There were no paramilitary or para-police units in Sokolac during the war. There were some informal groups of young men who terrorised both Muslims and Serbs, but with gradual establishment of authorities, these groups disappeared and these persons were expelled or arrested. There were no camps or prisons in Sokolac municipality, nor there were any instructions from the state authorities to set them up. Milovan Bjelica was aware of two incidents in June and September 1992 in which 50 and 44 civilians -- Muslim males had been killed. Regarding the incident in June, Milovan Bjelica only knew details of the incident after the exhumation of the bodies, because the incident was kept secret from the public. Regarding the second, Milovan Bjelica heard that it was committed by an informal group of Serbian youths, that the perpetrators covered up the crime, and that representatives of the Sokolac authorities were not informed about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you to tell us something about your relationship with the regional command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, i.e., the relationship of the civilian authorities and that military command. For example, in September or in the course of the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: May I? When it comes to the co-operation between the local civilian authorities of Sokolac municipality during that period of time, we had a Crisis Staff in the municipality of Sokolac. It was active sometime up to the month of June or July. After that, the Executive Board of Sokolac municipality was set up. The communication between the command of the 2nd Motorised Romanija Brigade and the local authorities in Sokolac municipality, i.e., the Executive Board and the president of the municipality, was not satisfactory. It was asked from the local authorities to provide additional funds for the military, primarily for the food, fuel, cigarettes, the food for the families of the combatants who were on the front line, because at that time people did not receive salaries, which is why food had to be supplied for the combatants as well as for their families. The authorities in Sokolac municipality requested from the brigade command to put a number of army members on standby to be given work obligation in the companies that were still open. They did not have enough trained and skilled workers for production, and that merely applies to the forestry and timber industry known as Romanija. We did not meet with the full understanding on the part of the command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade which resulted in misunderstandings. The command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade characterised this as interference with the line of control and command in the units of the Army of Republika Srpska, and it reported back to its superior command about that. We are going to see that document later on in the courtroom. The brigade commander reported back to his superior command with this regard. That's why the relationship between one part of the command on the one hand and the authorities of Sokolac municipality were not -- was not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up 1D07305. This is a document which is mentioned in paragraph 59. Please pay attention to this document. You have just mentioned something that I would like you to talk about. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: This is document -- the document that I have just mentioned. You can see that the command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade addressed its superior command, i.e., the Main Staff, and I can see from the document that it also contacted the Supreme Commander, i.e., the president of the Serbian Republic. It transpires from this document that the command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade informs them that civilian authorities should not interfere with the work of the military so that the political structures of Sokolac municipality cannot do that. They have their orders from the superior command that they were supposed to carry out and that they report only to the military leadership and the state leadership of Republika Srpska. Here they're trying to portray this as political interference, but it wasn't political interference. Things were just as I explained them in my previous answer before I was shown this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In English it is on the next page, and in Serbian it is the last paragraph here. The brigade commander claims that the SDS in Sokolac is also interfering and requesting that all of his activities should be subjected to the interest of the SDS. How correct is that, or is it just a matter of antagonism?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The SDS never interfered with the control and command of those units, because that was not within the party purview. The party purview was to encourage the local authorities to put in place conditions for a normal life of our combatants and the local population in Sokolac municipality. The situation was the same elsewhere. There was no interference whatsoever, and during that period the work of the Serbian Democratic Party was frozen. So we could not interfere on behalf of any party organs because it was you on a certain date, I don't know when exactly, sent us a directive. You sent it to the municipal structures of the Serbian Democratic Party to put the activities, political activities, of the party on hold, to suspend it for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll accept it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3232, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Crisis Staff? Did you know anything about the decisions that were made by the staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. I became a member of the Crisis Staff by virtue of my position on the day when it was set up. As far as I can remember, there were several persons who were members of the Crisis Staff by virtue of their duty. President of the municipality; the president of the Municipal Board of the SDS; the chief of the police station, the local police station in Sokolac, that is; chief of the Defence Department in the municipality; representatives of the industry, education, health care. Some were members and some attended the meetings of the Crisis Staff when needed. The members of the Crisis Staff were never from one party alone. There were also representatives of the other political parties in Sokolac that were a member of the Crisis Staff as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did the Crisis Staff deal with alcohol abuse and other risky behaviours that might have led to the escalation of the crisis and violence?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: We had such situations that certain individuals who returned from the front line arrived in settled areas with weapons. They would go to local pubs where they had one drink too many, and then they would use their firearms, i.e., they would open celebratory fire as we call it. In order to prevent such unfortunate events, to prevent those things that could lead to accidents, the Crisis Staff discussed the issue and issued orders to the effect that there would be a ban on serving alcohol in pubs and on carrying weapons in settled areas or on public premises. There was a ban of bringing weapons to any place where there might be larger groups of people present. So we did everything possible in order to prevent any unfortunate events that may have tragic consequences.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D4383. That document is mentioned in paragraph 79.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say celebratory shooting, where was fire most commonly opened?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: It could happen in a pub or around a pub, in places like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when fire was opened did they aim at anything?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: No. It was opened in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you look at the document and tell us whether that document is familiar to you? You mentioned a number of bans. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: This is exactly what I've just described. I'm familiar with the document, Mr. President. This is a document that the Crisis Staff issued -- or, rather, it adopted a decision and tasked the public security station in Sokolac with the implementation of this decision. Inspection services were tasked with the implementation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read for the benefit of the Trial Chamber paragraph 2. Can you please read it allowed.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: "All catering establishments in Sokolac must stop operating no later than 24 June 1992 at 1800 hours."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where is this document referred to? You said para 79?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. In paragraph 79 I see that it's document 5392. So we have to look a little bit further. I'm advised it's the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 65 ter number is different. It's 5392, whereas 1D is 4383.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I mean, I have no objection to it being MFI'd pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3233, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber when you finally managed to consolidate the municipal authorities during the first year of war, and to what extent could it control the developments there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The municipal authorities did everything in their power to maintain public order in the territory of our municipality and to provide for the security of citizens in Sokolac. However, it was a tall order. There was a lot of weapons. People returned from the front line. They were known to use weapons randomly from time to time. We tried to react. We had some shake-ups in the personnel of the public security station in Sokolac in order to improve the situation as best as we could. However, things were not intolerable, but our goal was prevention in order to avert any fatal consequences to the detriment of the security of the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In September 1992, did the Crisis Staff still function? What was the composition of the power in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in September 1992 the Executive Council of the municipality was already operational. As far as I can remember, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'd like to call up 1D7974. This document is mentioned in paragraph 81. I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 2 where it says: "There was a unanimous conclusion to the effect that in the territory of the municipality no legal regulations could be carried out or implemented because the public security station Sokolac is not functioning properly and because competent services cannot put a stop to lawlessness which is constantly on the rise." How do you interpret this, and how does this tally with what you know about the power or the impotence of the authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: That was already the time of an imminent threat of war which was declared. It was the area of responsibility of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, and the public security station in town controlled and made sure that laws were applied. However, we were not happy with the situation. There were a few incidents that involved a group of police reservists who controlled traffic at certain locations, and a number of citizens complained, which is why the Executive Council sent a request -- or, rather, a letter to the Ministry of the Interior which was headquartered in Pale, telling them that the situation had deteriorated and that it would be desirable to carry out a shake-up in the personnel in order to stop smuggling, thefts.
