We even had some armed attacks against individuals. There were also attacks at the public security station in Sokolac. Those attacks were carried out by certain individuals who jeopardised the functioning of the authorities, the implementation of the law, conclusions and orders by the Presidency of Republika Srpska. The lack of will power in the then public security station to prevent such incidents jeopardised the security of the citizens of Sokolac and threatened to lead to the state of anarchy. That's why we asked the Ministry of the Interior to help the local authorities to prevent this and to make sure that the citizens were safe in their town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What conclusions and orders by the Presidency of the republic are referred to that you had no power to implement them?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: For example, guaranteeing safety to all citizens residing in the territory of Sokolac municipality and protecting the functioning of the legal institutions of Republika Srpska at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Be it from the Presidency, the government, or the ministry, were any orders or instructions received that would distinguish between people based on their ethnic or religious background in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: No, never. Not a single document made us conclude at the time that there was any kind of discrimination aimed at anyone in particular or an ethnic group or an individual. That was never the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted, and paragraph 81 is the reference paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3234, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You just said that there was no difference in the way people were treated in the documents that were received in terms of distinguishing between the population in terms of religion or ethnicity. You also mentioned that people left some villages, some Muslims, whereas in other villages they stayed. Can you tell us what is the difference? Can you cite the villages in your municipality and neighbouring municipalities that were inhabited by Muslims who remained there, and what was the difference between those who left and those who stayed? To what extent did it depend on the decisions and conduct of the authorities, and what was their own behaviour?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The villages neighbouring Olovo that were part of the municipalities of Knezina and Kaljina at the beginning of the crisis and upon invitation of the then municipal president from Olovo Mr. Dzevad Abazovic were emptied. People moved to the territory of Olovo, and they took their cattle with them as well as whatever property they could take in order to find shelter, because there were front lines nearby, and so as to preserve their lives and property. That is why they responded to Dzevad Abazovic's call who came there together with the president of the Serb municipality of Olovo, Mr. Milovan Zugic. They came to Knezina to a meeting with the leadership of Sokolac municipality. On behalf of Sokolac municipality the meeting was attended by the Municipal President Mr. Milan Tupajic, president of the Executive Board of Sokolac municipality, the chief of prison station in Sokolac, and I think at the time the chief of the CSB of the Sarajevo-Romanija region Mr. Cvijetic. It was agreed that one part of the Muslim population move to the territory of Olovo, whereas another part or a part of the Serb residents move to the territory of Sokolac. That is what took place in the two local communes. In the villages of Novoseoci, Vrbarije, and Burati that were in the direction of Rogatica, the population remained there, and some remained even after the Dayton Accords were signed. Food was secured for them, and they had a designated shop where they could supply themselves with basic necessities which was as one enters Sokolac. It was agreed upon by the representatives of those villages with a municipal president. They could go there so as not to mingle with the rest of the population in town. We were afraid that if there were more of them in the town itself that it may result in casualties. We thought they would be safer at the entry point in Sokolac, although there were people who came to town individually buying what they needed. I know there were problems with working the land and harvesting. It was difficult to receive fuel, but Sokolac municipality did make it possible for the residents of those villages to have fuel as well that they could use for their agricultural machinery and whatever machinery was necessary for them to go about working their land.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Line 15 on this page, let us try and clarify something. You said that at an entry point to the town there was a shop that was dedicated to their supply so as not to mix with the refugees, whereas we seem to have victims in the town. Can you tell us what the risk was? What would be the risk of mixing these two populations and how many refugees were there in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: There were many refugees from Sarajevo and its municipalities such as Centar, Novi Grad, Hadzici, Stari Grad, Olovo, Kladanj, and some were from Zenica too. The risk was that they would mix with the families which had by that time during the war lost their members due to combat with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We -- it was an attempt to suppress any kind of provocation or retaliation aimed at the Muslim population. That was the reason for their personal safety, because by that time we had had at least several dozen victims of Serbian ethnicity in the territory of our municipality, and those who came from Sarajevo and Olovo, some of them lost their nearest and dearest as well. In Sokolac itself during the war, there were some 1.300 killed soldiers and civilians who were buried during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Vrbarije. Until what time did the residents, Muslim residents of Vrbarije remain living in their village near Sokolac? When did people leave and how?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I cannot recall a specific date, but I know that they remained for a few years at least in their village and that they co-operated well with their neighbours. Once they decided to go when the crisis was -- well, the situation was very difficult by that time. It was difficult to secure food and other necessities. Then a number of them decided to go to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina controlled territory. This was arranged with international organisations. I think it was the ICRC that was involved in it. As far as I know, it was reported on by TV crews. It was recorded by the Serb radio and TV as well as by foreign crews. It was broadcast in the media where people could see how they left and bidding farewell with their Serb neighbours, and both sides were crying and kissing, et cetera. Once the crisis was over they returned, and as far as I know to date they live well with their neighbours, aiding each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the arranged move between Knezevo and Olovo, was it on a permanent basis or was it temporary, and were there any returns there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: It was on a temporary basis. I've said already that it was to provide shelter for them for the time being in the municipalities of Knezina, Olovo, and Kaljina. By that time there were incidents on the borders of those municipalities. It was also for the sake of Serb civilians for Olovo to find shelter in RS territory. It was initiated by the Olovo municipal president, a Bosniak Muslim, Mr. Dzevad Abazovic. That move looking from this position was a good one, because most of them surprised. A number of Serbs returned to Olovo, and most of the Bosniaks returned to their property and hearts. They had left both with the cattle and whatever property they could take temporarily, and they returned immediately following the Dayton Peace Accords. They still live there and their children attend schools there, although there aren't too many of their children theirs there. In any case, they are religiously active and their co-operation with their neighbours is a good one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Abazovic, what party did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: As far as I know, the did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D7991. I think we have the subtitles in English so that we can follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What party was he? You said he was the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Abazovic was in the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now see this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "This is the village of Vrbarije near Sokolac in Bosnia inhabited mainly by Serbs and Muslims. After the imposed Dayton Peace Accords, the villagers were aware of what this meant to them. And as the town became part of the Serb entity, the Muslims decided to collectively leave to their own entity "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Both of you are in tears. Neighbours, today you are parting ways. "That we are. "Well, is it hard? "Yes, as you can see two neighbours saying goodbye in tears. "From the depth of my hard and his. Definitely. "Definitely. "You lived together for so many years. "As many years as he's lived, together for 68 years without fights or disagreements, always helping each other our entire lives and now as well. "And how is it now? "It's hard. "Was there any abuse by the other side? Was it bad for you here? "Never. It couldn't have been better. "Are you sad? "Of course I'm sad. We're saying goodbye to our neighbours. We've always liked them. We got along great. "Did the Serb kids ever provoke you or cause any problems? "No, never. Everything between us was good, just like before. "No disagreements, no pressures, no fights? "No, never, never here. "You're alive and well? "Alive and well. Never had the slightest problem. Lots of people came, soldiers, different ethnic groups. Nobody even gave me a dirty look. Our neighbours are here. We're all crying. We're saying goodbye the way human beings should. "I want things to be like before, for problems to get fixed so we can live together again. I want Yugoslavia back like it was before."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is stated that these people left after the agreement, after their village became part of the Serb entity. During the war were any of these people killed or were any Serbs killed by these people?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: None of them were killed. There were cases close to their villages, perhaps not in the village itself, a mine was laid or mines, and upon return following a funeral when Ilija Macar and his wife were coming back, they came across those mines near the village and were both killed. However, no one ever blamed the people who lived there for it, because we realized that it was some kind of provocation. It was so clarified to me, and that those people should not pay for that. They continued being treated the same way. You can see that they are well fed and clothed as they left. And they returned after a while, perhaps a few years later after the Dayton Accords were signed. They still work on their land today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelica. I didn't say that, but I suppose that we will find it in the statement. You are the mayor of Sokolac today; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were elected by direct ballot; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender the video-clip into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I've got a number of objections to the video-clip. Firstly, the witness wasn't asked any questions about the actual clip, so he wasn't asked to recognise anything or whether he'd seen this before or what it depicted, so there's just a basic lack of foundation for its admission. In addition, we were informed that this clip comes from a movie called "The Weight of Chains" that from what we can gather on the internet was created in 2010 that appears to take a clip from a source that is not apparent on the video, so we don't know where the original footage comes from. I also note that in the first few seconds of the video the commentator states that: "After the imposed Dayton Peace Accords, the villagers were aware of what this meant to them, and as the town became part of the Serb entity, the Muslims decided to collectively leave to their own entity." Now, that is directly contradictory to the accused's own case on what happened to these villagers. He tendered with the previous witness from Sokolac D3189, which is the document from the Sokolac SJB to the Sarajevo CJB stating that the 61 civilians from Vrbarije were transferred to Kula prison in October of 1994, which is well over a year before the Dayton Peace Accords, and this witness has said in his statement, and again he indicated in his testimony, that these people left in 1994 and in his testimony just now he said they returned sometime after the Dayton Peace Accords. So there are some serious concerns about the reliability of this video and for those reasons we object to its admission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I clarify things with the witness? First of all, the witness did mention Vrbarije on several occasions. Second of all, he mentioned that some people left in 1994 and that some left after Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, do you know who actually recorded this footage at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, I can see Mr. Skiljevic who was a TV journalist. He was affiliated with the radio television of Republika Srpska. I can also see Ms. Suzanna Obradovic who was also a journalist. I can see Milomir Vitomir, Nedzo Vitomir, Mr. Kadri, and some others whom I know. I'm familiar with this. I was not there, I was not on the spot, but I'm sure that this is an authentic document which aired on the media. I commented upon this document in the Krajisnik case. The document was original. I was a Defence witness for Mr. Krajisnik. It was sometime in April 2006. And this video-clip was shown and tendered into evidence in that case. Perhaps it was not the same version, 2010. It was the authentic document which aired on radio television and there was another international channel that aired that same programme. I don't know which one. The journalists are Skiljevic, Obradovic, Vitomir, Djokics, and the others whom you can see kissing their neighbours and saying their good-byes to them. I've already told you that some of the locals left before the Dayton Accords, some left after the Dayton Accords, but they all returned. Sixty or so people left on that day, but nobody ever killed in either Vrbarije or Burate. Those are two villages bordering on Sokolac and Rogatica or rather halfway between Sokolac and Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, is this enough? The video-clip was edited later, and in 2006 it was shown before this Tribunal in a different case as the original footage that was shown on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is part of movie which is called "Weight of Chains"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was used subsequently as a document in 2010, whereas in 2006 [Realtime transcript read in error "1996"] Mr. Bjelica used this document in the courtroom when it was not part of the whole show. I keep on repeating 2006 and it keeps on being recorded as 1996. 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not clear from Mr. Bjelica's answer who filmed this and when.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian Radio Television. He said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you help us, Mr. Bjelica? Which channel produced this clip? And you already told us about the journalists.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The Serbian Radio Television and Radio Romanija produced this video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: On the day when they left. It was shot on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When was it, Mr. Bjelica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may have been sometime in late 1995 or early 1996. After the Dayton Accords were signed in any case. I can't give you the exact date, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just two remarks. Dr. Karadzic's answer wasn't clear, but I assume the Defence will agree as they told me this this morning that this video-clip we just saw came from a movie called "Weight of Chains" which, as I said, from the internet appears to have been created in 2010. Also, Dr. Karadzic has picked up on Mr. Bjelica's assertion that this video was played in the Krajisnik. It certainly wasn't played in court in the Krajisnik case because I have recently read Mr. Bjelica's testimony in the Krajisnik case several times and there is no video played. So I don't know where that comes from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I'm right and that I understood Mr. Bjelica who said that he used the information from that film. That film existed in 1995, and it became part of the documentary in 2010. That's how documentaries are made. The existing materials are used and compiled in order to make up a documentary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the Chamber has sufficient a foundational provenance of this film to be admitted at this stage. Until that time, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3235, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I have some -- you have some further questions, but we'll do that tomorrow given the time, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, your Excellency. I am done with my examination-in-chief. I believe that Mr. Peter Robinson will be able to understand the concerns about these excerpts and we will be able to obtain more information or maybe a better copy from the TV house that produced it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you not tendering 1D14014?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. Everything that we have led live is being tendered into evidence. A total of three documents and the video-clip that we've just seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We should lead that live tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bjelica, before we do, how do you spell your last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I spell it for you? B-j-e-l-i-c-a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. There's no i before j. That's what I wanted to confirm with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there's no i.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn for today and continue tomorrow. Can I advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 3rd day of April, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.52 p.m.,
